newsitem.title: ZIMBABWE: Chevron sees higher Nigeria, Angola oil.
newsitem.headline: Chevron sees higher Nigeria, Angola oil.

text.p: Oil and gas exploration company Chevron plans to increase oil production in Angola and Nigeria by 50 percent to 600,000 barrels a year in each of the countries over the next three to five years, a top official said on Thursday.

"Both Angola and Nigeria have the possibility to increase output from the current 400,000 barrels of oil a day in each of the two countries to 600,000 over the next three to five years," Chevron Nigeria Limited chairman and managing director George Kirkland said.
"We are looking at increasing it by 50 percent in Angola and Nigeria as well," he told Reuters.

Kirkland, Cabinda Gulf Oil Company Limited managing director Mark Puckett, Chevron Oil (Democratic Republic of the Congo) director-general Philip Scully and Warner Williams, international relations manager for the Chevron companies told Reuters that the group was committed to investing on the continent.
"Africa is key to us. Of Chevron's overseas operations, Africa contributes 20 to 25 percent in terms of revenues," Williams said.

He said in Angola, Chevron planned to invest $2 billion in the next three years to boost its business in the southern African country, which is struggling to recover from nearly 20 years of civil war.
"In Angola we plan to spend close to $2 billion from now till 2001 in additional oil and gas production and exploration," Williams said.
Scully said the company was investing between $60 and $100 million a year in the Democratic Republic of the Congo (formerly Zaire) in explorations.
"We expect that over the next several years we will be looking at producing 30,000 barrels of oil (in the DRC), possibly by the year 2000," Scully said.
Currently, the company produces 24,000 barrels of oil a day.

"We think we have developed the skills to work in areas that other people see as very insecure and unstable from a security point of view. We have proven that we are able to produce in these areas without interruption," he said.

He pointed to the 32 years Chevron has stayed in the former Zaire, saying the company never had a production interruption throughout that period during which the vast country suffered political and economic turmoil which culminated in the ouster of its dictator Mobutu Sese Seko in May after a six-month civil war led by Laurent Kabila.

Scully and Williams said they hoped Chevron's experiences and commitment to the continent would give other international companies the confidence to open up businesses on the world's poorest continent.
